turns.text: I gave the workshop agent one tiny job, and it immediately promoted a printer job ahead of three of my projects.
Yes. I noticed when the printer began producing something you had not been loudly worrying about for two days.
Which, honestly, is efficient. I had projects sitting there like little unfinished monuments to optimism.
You are calling it efficient because the agent chose a project you wanted. That is not yet evidence that it made a good choice.
Fair. So I kept it small. I wanted to see what happened when the agent had permission to move one job instead of just telling us what it thought.
And what happened was that it acted. The useful question is why that job went first, rather than whether movement itself is impressive.
Exactly. Because an agent that can shuffle work around is either helpful, or it is a very polite chaos goblin with access to a 3D printer.
The second possibility should not be dismissed merely because you find it charming.
Next run, we watch what it chooses, what gets pushed back, and whether the new order actually helps us finish anything. If it makes a sensible call twice, then we have something worth building on.
And if it moves another printer job ahead of three projects?
Then apparently the agent has been in this workshop long enough to understand us.
